prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints and asset prices amplify and propagate shocks, and thereby explaining credit-driven economic fluctuations

statement.case_for: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) give a compact dynamic general-equilibrium mechanism in which credit limits depend on collateral values and collateral values depend on credit. Small or temporary shocks therefore become large and persistent, and this feedback is the basis of most modern macro-financial models. The mechanism is general, tractable and testable, and it has been extended for nearly three decades, including in the quantitative models used to analyse 2007-09 and later episodes. It is also a clean two-person attribution, because the originating paper is a joint contribution of exactly these two authors. I weigh it on those grounds. Its position at the top of several colleagues' rankings is not itself evidence of merit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with the 2022 prize for work on banks and financial crises (Bernanke, Diamond, Dybvig). A committee could read credit-cycle amplification as an adjacent theme that is already honoured. The empirical identification of the collateral channel is also more indirect than the theory suggests. A second concern is the boundary with the financial-accelerator tradition (Gertler, Gilchrist). Keeping that tradition out leaves a real part of the credit-frictions story unrecognised.

responses.point: Enflo proposes adding Mark Gertler as a third laureate on B011. Her reasoning is that the Gertler line of work built the Kiyotaki-Moore mechanism into quantitative macro models used in policy. She also flags that Bernanke's 2022 prize covers part of the accelerator lineage.
responses.response: I take the point that quantitative implementation matters, and Gertler's independent contributions are real. But I still prefer two names. The accelerator is a distinct mechanism, based on balance-sheet and external-finance premium effects, and not the collateral-price feedback of the 1997 paper. The part of it most associated with Bernanke was already recognised in 2022. Adding Gertler would blur the discovery being honoured and import the very overlap that Enflo and I both see as the main risk. It would also create an attribution entanglement, because Gertler is a leading name in B019. I would revisit this if colleagues argue that the accelerator and collateral-feedback strands cannot be separated for citation purposes.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B001 (Mian and Sufi) first. His case is that household leverage and credit-supply expansions explain housing booms and busts with credible granular evidence, and that the work is ripe and highly policy-relevant. He ranks Kiyotaki-Moore only seventh because of overlap with the 2022 prize and with B001.
responses.response: I agree that the Mian-Sufi evidence is credible and important, and I ranked it third. But the two candidates differ in what they establish. Kiyotaki-Moore supply the general mechanism, and Mian-Sufi supply the empirical demonstration of one channel through which household balance sheets matter in a specific episode. Much of the Mian-Sufi interpretation relies on mechanisms of the kind Kiyotaki and Moore formalised. That argues for treating the mechanism as more foundational and, with its longer record, as more mature. Boppart's overlap concern with the 2022 prize applies to both candidates, so I do not think it favours B001. His point about maturity is fair, though. The Mian-Sufi evidence is younger, and the debate about the causal weight of credit supply is not settled, so I keep B001 as an alternative and not as the preferred part.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B005 (Helpman and Melitz) first. He argues that heterogeneous-firm trade theory is foundational and general, with over two decades of confirmation across many datasets, and that the timing is ripe.
responses.response: I agree on maturity and generality, and B005 was my second choice. The framework changed how the field models and measures trade. Where I differ is on the incremental case. Helpman's earlier contributions overlap with the new trade theory recognised in 2008, and attribution around Melitz is contested by Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, who are not credited on this entry. Because of that, the citation for B005 is harder to draw cleanly than the two-author B011 citation. That is a judgement about attribution, not a claim that the science is weaker. I would support B005 as the alternative, and I would want the committee to discuss the Helpman-Melitz boundary explicitly if it moves in that direction.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the collateral-feedback mechanism as sufficiently distinct from the work recognised in 2022, or as adjacent territory already honoured.
Whether the financial-accelerator contributions of Gertler and Gilchrist can be separated from Kiyotaki-Moore for citation purposes, or whether a two-name award would be seen as incomplete.
How much weight the committee should give to the indirect empirical identification of the collateral channel compared with the strength of the theory.
For B005, how the committee would resolve attribution among Helpman, Melitz and the empirical-trade contributors not credited on that entry.
statement.conflict_note: The supplied profile shows no connection to any credited name on B011, B005 or B001. It does show frequent co-authorship with Per Krusell, who ranked B011 first, and co-authorship with Timo Boppart and Richard Friberg, whose arguments I address above. These are connections to colleagues, not to candidates. I note them for transparency and do not treat agreement or disagreement with them as evidence of merit.
